title: 7.2.12 Lab: Three Enemies in three variables
description: Instantiate e1, e2, and e3 from the Enemy class at three different positions: three independent instances, each in its own named variable.

steps.title: Create e1, e2, e3 at three different positions
steps.instructions: In `setup()`, create three Enemy instances: `e1`, `e2`, and `e3`, at three different x/y positions. Each call to `new Enemy(x, y, hp)` produces a separate object with its own state.
hints: Open the moSHion docs drawer on the right and review how constructor arguments work: each Enemy takes an x, y, and hp value.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "7.2.12 Lab: Three Enemies in three variables". The task they were given: An Enemy class is given: new Enemy(x, y, hp) stores hp and builds a red square sprite. The starter declares let e1, e2, e3 at the top. In setup(), create three Enemy instances, e1, e2 and e3, at three different positions; draw() calls render() on each so its hp shows on its square. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. Each new Enemy(...) call makes a separate object with its own hp and its own sprite. draw() reads the e1, e2 and e3 declared at the top of the file. Writing let or const in front of the name again inside setup() makes a new variable that only setup() can see, so draw()'s variable stays empty and that enemy's hp label never appears. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, ternaries or if-chains, semicolons, spacing, quotes, order and helper functions of their own are all fine; only a name the starter's own code already calls or reads has to keep that name. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or a string never runs, so the starter's STEP comments are never the student's work. Any positions and hp values count; different positions are what step 1 asks, so all three squares can be seen. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise. Write for a 14-year-old beginner: short sentences and everyday words.
